introduction: On this second Sunday of Easter, Divine Mercy Sunday, the risen Jesus comes through locked doors, gives his disciples peace and breathes the Holy Spirit on them for the forgiveness of sins. Thomas, who doubted, makes the greatest confession of faith in the Gospels. The first believers share everything they have. Let us welcome the mercy of the risen Lord, and let it shape the way we live together.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the risen Lord stands among us and says, Peace be to you. Let us pray to the Father of mercies.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be a place where all find the mercy of God and the peace of the risen Christ. Let us pray to the Lord.
For priests who hear confessions: that they may be faithful ministers of the forgiveness Jesus entrusted to his apostles. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who doubt or struggle to believe: that the risen Lord may meet them, as he met Thomas. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the poor and all in need: that Christian communities may share their goods so that no one among them lacks what they need. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may receive God's mercy in the sacrament of Reconciliation and show mercy to others. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Merciful Father, your Son breathed his Spirit on the apostles for the forgiveness of sins. Make us witnesses of your mercy, and keep us one in heart and soul. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: My Lord and my God
reflection.body:
On the evening of the first Easter, the disciples are behind locked doors, afraid. Jesus comes and stands among them and says, "Peace be to you." He shows them his hands and his side, and "The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord." Then he sends them: "As the Father has sent me, even so I send you."

He breathes on them and gives them a gift for the whole Church: "Receive the Holy Spirit! If you forgive anyone's sins, they have been forgiven them." The first gift of the risen Lord is forgiveness. That is why this Sunday, since Saint John Paul II established it in 2000, is also called Divine Mercy Sunday.

Thomas was not there. He wants proof, and he sets his conditions. A week later Jesus comes again and offers him exactly what he asked for: "Reach here your finger, and see my hands." Thomas does not need to touch. He simply says, "My Lord and my God!" The one who doubted makes the clearest confession of faith in John's Gospel. And Jesus speaks to us: "Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed."

The first reading shows what this faith does to a community. "The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul," and they shared everything, so that no one among them was in need. Mercy received becomes mercy shared.

John tells us why he wrote his Gospel: "that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name." This week, bring your own doubts honestly to the Lord, as Thomas did. If it has been a long time since your last confession, let this be the week. And look for one concrete way to share with someone in need.
